A 74.6% loss demands a 294% rebound just to break even; cutting that drawdown to 27.8% with XLV cuts the needed rebound to 38.5%.

Quick Dollar Drawdown Estimator (2000–2025 Historical Data)

Compound arithmetic punishes deep drawdowns asymmetrically. Lose 20% and you need 25% to climb back. Lose 75% and your remaining capital must quadruple (+300%) merely to return to your original statement balance.

That simple math explains why a 100% semiconductor allocation, despite impressive long-run revenue growth, trailed a calmer balanced mix on a risk-adjusted basis over 25 years. Every deep cycle forces panicked savers out near the bottom.

Healthcare (XLV) acts as an unleveraged earnings stabilizer rather than a dead weight. Between 2000 and 2025, XLV compounded steadily on its own while absorbing less than half the peak drop of semiconductors.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does adding XLV permanently drag down long-term returns?

Across 2000–2025 historical spot series, semi-annual rebalancing between SMH and XLV actually captured volatility harvesting: trimming overheated chips into healthcare before busts and re-centering after crashes.

Why not use long-term Treasury bonds (TLT) instead of XLV?

In 2022, long-duration Treasury bonds fell over 30% simultaneously with tech equities because rising inflation hurt both. Healthcare cash flows and 0–3 month T-bills (SGOV) avoided long-duration bond shock.
